claim: Mutant RHO is the most frequent genetic cause of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (adRP).
source: Mutant RHO is the most frequent genetic cause of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (adRP).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the genetic causes of adRP.

claim: An allele-specific gene-editing therapeutic drug was developed to selectively target the human T17M RHO mutant allele while leaving the wild-type RHO allele intact for the first time.
source: Here, we developed an allele-specific gene-editing therapeutic drug to selectively target the human T17M RHO mutant allele while leaving the wild-type RHO allele intact for the first time.
evidence: This is the primary claim of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A Staphylococcus aureus Cas9 (SaCas9) guide RNA was identified that was highly active and specific to the human T17M RHO allele.
source: We identified a Staphylococcus aureus Cas9 (SaCas9) guide RNA that was highly active and specific to the human T17M RHO allele.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro and in vivo experimental data showing specificity and activity.

claim: In vitro experiments using HEK293T cells demonstrated active nuclease activity and high specificity.
source: In vitro experiments using HEK293T cells and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) demonstrated active nuclease activity and high specificity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from T7E1 assays, TA cloning, and western blotting shown in Figure 2.

claim: In vitro experiments using patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) demonstrated active nuclease activity and high specificity.
source: In vitro experiments using HEK293T cells and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) demonstrated active nuclease activity and high specificity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from patient-derived iPSCs shown in Figure 3.

claim: Subretinal delivery of a single adeno-associated virus serotype 2/8 packaging SaCas9 and single guide RNA (sgRNA) to the retinas of the RHO humanized mice showed that this therapeutic drug targeted the mutant allele selectively.
source: Subretinal delivery of a single adeno-associated virus serotype 2/8 packaging SaCas9 and single guide RNA (sgRNA) to the retinas of the RHO humanized mice showed that this therapeutic drug targeted the mutant allele selectively, thereby downregulating the mutant RHO mRNA expression.
evidence: This is supported by T7E1 assays, Hi-Tom sequencing, and PCR-based NGS data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The therapeutic drug downregulated the mutant RHO mRNA expression in RHO humanized mice.
source: Subretinal delivery of a single adeno-associated virus serotype 2/8 packaging SaCas9 and single guide RNA (sgRNA) to the retinas of the RHO humanized mice showed that this therapeutic drug targeted the mutant allele selectively, thereby downregulating the mutant RHO mRNA expression.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and sequencing data showing decreased mutant mRNA levels in Figure 7.

claim: Administration of this therapeutic drug resulted in a long-term (up to 11 months after treatment) improvement of retinal function in the heterozygous mutant humanized mice.
source: Administration of this therapeutic drug resulted in a long-term (up to 11 months after treatment) improvement of retinal function and preservation of photoreceptors in the heterozygous mutant humanized mice.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data at 11 months post-injection shown in Figure 8.

claim: Administration of this therapeutic drug resulted in preservation of photoreceptors in the heterozygous mutant humanized mice for up to 11 months after treatment.
source: Administration of this therapeutic drug resulted in a long-term (up to 11 months after treatment) improvement of retinal function and preservation of photoreceptors in the heterozygous mutant humanized mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 9.

claim: The study demonstrated a dose-dependent therapeutic effect in vivo.
source: Our study demonstrated a dose-dependent therapeutic effect in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing effects at different AAV doses (5×10^8, 1×10^9, and 3×10^9) shown in Figures 5, 7, 8, and 9.

claim: Unwanted off-target effects were not observed at the whole-genome sequencing level.
source: Unwanted off-target effects were not observed at the whole-genome sequencing level.
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is one of the most common causes of blindness in industrialized countries.
source: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP [MIM:268000]), a subtype of inherited retinal dystrophies (IRDs), is one of the most common causes of blindness in industrialized countries, with an incidence of 1 in 1000 in North China (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2006.

claim: The incidence of retinitis pigmentosa is 1 in 1000 in North China.
source: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP [MIM:268000]), a subtype of inherited retinal dystrophies (IRDs), is one of the most common causes of blindness in industrialized countries, with an incidence of 1 in 1000 in North China (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2006.

claim: There are currently no reliable therapies available to cure or delay the disease progression of RP.
source: However, there are currently no reliable therapies available to cure or delay the disease progression of RP.
evidence: This is a statement of current clinical knowledge about RP treatment options.

claim: In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved Luxturna, an adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy drug for RPE65-associated Leber's Congenital Amaurosis (RPE65-LCA).
source: In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved Luxturna, an adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy drug for RPE65-associated Leber's Congenital Amaurosis (RPE65-LCA) (Russell et al., 2017; Smalley, 2017), which marked the start of gene therapy for IRDs (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Russell et al., 2017 and Smalley, 2017.

claim: The approval of Luxturna marked the start of gene therapy for inherited retinal dystrophies.
source: In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved Luxturna, an adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy drug for RPE65-associated Leber's Congenital Amaurosis (RPE65-LCA) (Russell et al., 2017; Smalley, 2017), which marked the start of gene therapy for IRDs (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2019.

claim: Mutations in the human rhodopsin (RHO) gene are the most prominent genetic causes of autosomal dominant RP (adRP), accounting for about 30% of adRP cases.
source: Mutations in the human rhodopsin (RHO) gene are the most prominent genetic causes of autosomal dominant RP (adRP), accounting for about 30% of adRP cases (Iannaccone et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Iannaccone et al., 2006.

claim: RHO-adRP is mainly caused by a gain-of-function or dominant-negative mutation.
source: However, different from the RPE65-LCA, which is caused by a loss-of-function mutation, RHO-adRP is mainly caused by a gain-of-function or dominant-negative mutation (Li et al., 2018; Mendes et al., 2005), thereby restricting the application of gene replacement therapy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Mendes et al., 2005.

claim: The gain-of-function or dominant-negative nature of RHO mutations restricts the application of gene replacement therapy.
source: However, different from the RPE65-LCA, which is caused by a loss-of-function mutation, RHO-adRP is mainly caused by a gain-of-function or dominant-negative mutation (Li et al., 2018; Mendes et al., 2005), thereby restricting the application of gene replacement therapy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanistic difference between loss-of-function and gain-of-function mutations.

claim: Allele-independent gene ablation techniques have been studied for the treatment of RHO-adRP.
source: Many studies have been conducted regarding the treatment technique for RHO-adRP, such as allele-independent gene ablation. This technique includes silencing the expression of both the mutant RHO allele and its wild-type (WT) counterpart and simultaneously adding an exogenous WT RHO gene beyond the regulation of the retina in vivo (Mitra et al., 2018; Cideciyan et al., 2018; Tsai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mitra et al., 2018; Cideciyan et al., 2018; Tsai et al., 2018.

claim: Many risks remain with the disruption of the WT allele in allele-independent gene ablation approaches.
source: Although these methods are applicable to RHO-adRP, many risks remain with the disruption of the WT allele.
evidence: This is a statement based on scientific reasoning about the potential consequences of disrupting the wild-type allele.

claim: Allele-specific methods have been used extensively to treat adRP.
source: Recently, allele-specific methods have been used extensively to treat adRP (Meng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2020.

claim: Allele-specific RHO gene downregulation at the RNA level using antisense oligonucleotides (ASO), short hairpin RNA, or RNA interference can be achieved.
source: With the aim of allele-specific RHO gene downregulation at the RNA level using antisense oligonucleotides (ASO), short hairpin RNA, or RNA interference (Meng et al., 2020) can be achieved, some of which have been translated into clinical trials.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2020.

claim: Some allele-specific RNA-level approaches have been translated into clinical trials.
source: With the aim of allele-specific RHO gene downregulation at the RNA level using antisense oligonucleotides (ASO), short hairpin RNA, or RNA interference (Meng et al., 2020) can be achieved, some of which have been translated into clinical trials.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2020.

claim: Repeated treatments, especially for subretinal injections, are bound to hamper therapeutic effectiveness of RNA-level approaches.
source: However, repeated treatments, especially for subretinal injections, are bound to hamper therapeutic effectiveness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the practical limitations of repeated invasive procedures.

claim: Allele-specific mutant DNA targeting approaches with the CRISPR/Cas9 system, which leads to permanent DNA modification, may be more promising than RNA-level approaches.
source: In comparison, allele-specific mutant DNA targeting approaches, specifically with the CRISPR/Cas9 system (Mali et al., 2013; Ran et al., 2015), which leads to permanent DNA modification, may be more promising.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to Mali et al., 2013 and Ran et al., 2015.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas9 system has been used extensively to treat adRP caused by RHO-P23H, S334ter, P347S mutations.
source: In fact, the CRISPR/Cas9 system has been used extensively to treat adRP caused by RHO-P23H, S334ter, P347S mutations, etc. This resulted in the delay in photoreceptor degeneration and rescue of retinal function in animal models (Latella et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018; Giannelli et al., 2018; Patrizi et al., 2021; Bakondi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Latella et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018; Giannelli et al., 2018; Patrizi et al., 2021; Bakondi et al., 2016.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 treatment resulted in the delay in photoreceptor degeneration and rescue of retinal function in animal models of RHO-adRP.
source: In fact, the CRISPR/Cas9 system has been used extensively to treat adRP caused by RHO-P23H, S334ter, P347S mutations, etc. This resulted in the delay in photoreceptor degeneration and rescue of retinal function in animal models (Latella et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018; Giannelli et al., 2018; Patrizi et al., 2021; Bakondi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Latella et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018; Giannelli et al., 2018; Patrizi et al., 2021; Bakondi et al., 2016.

claim: Previous proof-of-concept CRISPR/Cas9 studies for RHO-adRP are not suitable for direct translation into clinical practice.
source: However, these proof-of-concept studies are not suitable for direct translation into clinical practice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of previous studies.

claim: There is currently no approved treatment for adRP.
source: Therefore, there is currently no approved treatment for adRP.
evidence: This is a statement of current clinical knowledge.

claim: The P23H mutation is the most common RHO mutation in North America, accounting for 10% of adRP cases due to a founder effect.
source: The P23H mutation is the most common RHO mutation in North America, accounting for 10% of adRP cases due to a founder effect, while it has not been reported elsewhere, including Europe and Asia (Meng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2020.

claim: The P23H mutation has not been reported in Europe and Asia.
source: The P23H mutation is the most common RHO mutation in North America, accounting for 10% of adRP cases due to a founder effect, while it has not been reported elsewhere, including Europe and Asia (Meng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2020.

claim: Some Chinese adRP patients carried RHO-T17M mutation.
source: Data gathered from our previous study (Liu et al., 2021) showed that some Chinese adRP patients carried RHO-T17M mutation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: T17M is one of the most common RHO mutations.
source: Several studies and data from the Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD, http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/ac/index.php) also prove that T17M (Sheffield, 1991; Krebs et al., 2010; Rakoczy et al., 2011) is one of the most common RHO mutations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sheffield, 1991; Krebs et al., 2010; Rakoczy et al., 2011 and reference to HGMD database.

claim: If the disease-causing allele has unique protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) sequences that are not present in the WT allele, the disease-causing allele may be discriminated from its WT counterpart.
source: Previous in vitro and in vivo studies have shown that if the disease-causing allele has unique protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) sequences that are not present in the WT allele, or when the mutations are within the spacer region of the Cas9/single guide RNA (sgRNA) target site, the disease-causing allele may be discriminated from its WT counterpart.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about CRISPR/Cas9 specificity mechanisms.

claim: When mutations are within the spacer region of the Cas9/sgRNA target site, the disease-causing allele may be discriminated from its WT counterpart.
source: Previous in vitro and in vivo studies have shown that if the disease-causing allele has unique protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) sequences that are not present in the WT allele, or when the mutations are within the spacer region of the Cas9/single guide RNA (sgRNA) target site, the disease-causing allele may be discriminated from its WT counterpart.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about CRISPR/Cas9 specificity mechanisms.

claim: The aim of selectively inactivating the mutant allele while leaving the WT ones functionally intact can be achieved using allele-specific CRISPR/Cas9.
source: Therefore, the aim of selectively inactivating the mutant allele while leaving the WT ones functionally intact can be achieved (Burnight et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Giannelli et al., 2018; Patrizi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burnight et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Giannelli et al., 2018; Patrizi et al., 2021.

claim: Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the primary mechanism for double-strand breaks in terminally differentiated rod cells.
source: Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the primary mechanism for double-strand breaks in terminally differentiated rod cells, whereas homologous recombination commonly occurs in mitotic cells such as induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) or HEK293T (293T) (Chan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2011.

claim: Homologous recombination commonly occurs in mitotic cells such as induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) or HEK293T.
source: Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the primary mechanism for double-strand breaks in terminally differentiated rod cells, whereas homologous recombination commonly occurs in mitotic cells such as induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) or HEK293T (293T) (Chan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2011.

claim: The difference in DNA repair mechanisms between rod cells and mitotic cells emphasizes the significance and necessity of performing experiments in vivo, especially in humanized animal models.
source: This difference in rod cells from mitotic cells emphasizes the significance and necessity of performing experiments in vivo, especially in humanized animal models.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanistic differences in DNA repair between cell types.

claim: Allele-specific CRISPR/Cas9 experiments have not been performed in humanized animal models prior to this study.
source: Unfortunately, allele-specific CRISPR/Cas9 experiments have not been performed in humanized animal models.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: 17-Sg1 and -Sg2 appeared to preferentially cut the mutant sequence, but not the WT sequence.
source: 17-Sg1 and -Sg2 appeared to preferentially cut the mutant sequence, but not the WT sequence, whereas 17-Sg3 cut both the WT and mutant sequences and appeared to cut the mutant sequence more than the WT sequence (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro digestion assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 17-Sg3 cut both the WT and mutant sequences and appeared to cut the mutant sequence more than the WT sequence.
source: 17-Sg1 and -Sg2 appeared to preferentially cut the mutant sequence, but not the WT sequence, whereas 17-Sg3 cut both the WT and mutant sequences and appeared to cut the mutant sequence more than the WT sequence (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro digestion assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: T7E1 assay for RHO17 cells transfected with 17-Sg1 or -Sg2 plasmid demonstrated that 17-Sg1 and -Sg2 were able to specifically cut the mutant sequence.
source: In contrast, the T7E1 assay for RHO17 cells transfected with 17-Sg1 or -Sg2 plasmid demonstrated that 17-Sg1 and -Sg2 were able to specifically cut the mutant sequence (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by T7E1 assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Indels were found at frequencies of 11.86% (7/59) in samples of SaCas9/17-Sg1.
source: Indels were not detected in WT samples. However, indels were found at frequencies of 11.86% (7/59) and 25.42% (15/59) in samples of SaCas9/17-Sg1 and SaCas9/17-Sg2, respectively (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1a).

claim: Indels were found at frequencies of 25.42% (15/59) in samples of SaCas9/17-Sg2.
source: Indels were not detected in WT samples. However, indels were found at frequencies of 11.86% (7/59) and 25.42% (15/59) in samples of SaCas9/17-Sg1 and SaCas9/17-Sg2, respectively (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by TA cloning and Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Rhodopsin expression in RHO17 cells transfected with 17-Sg1 or -Sg2 plasmid was strongly reduced compared to the counterpart of RHOwt cells with 17-Sg1 or -Sg2 plasmid.
source: Moreover, we evaluated rhodopsin protein production through western blotting (WB). Rhodopsin expression in RHO17 cells transfected with 17-Sg1 or -Sg2 plasmid was strongly reduced compared to the counterpart of RHOwt cells with 17-Sg1 or -Sg2 plasmid (Figure 2D–E).

claim: The mCherry/GFP ratio in 17-Sg1 and 17-Sg2 cells transfected with the RHO17 plasmid was significantly reduced compared to that of Lenti-CTRL cells transfected with the RHO17 plasmid.
source: The mCherry/GFP ratio in 17-Sg1 and 17-Sg2 cells transfected with the RHO17 plasmid was significantly reduced compared to that of Lenti-CTRL cells transfected with the RHO17 plasmid (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E).

claim: SaCas9/17-Sg1 and SaCas9/17-Sg2 enabled discrimination between WT and mutant alleles, targeting the mutant allele exclusively.
source: These results evidently indicated that SaCas9/17-Sg1 and SaCas9/17-Sg2 enabled discrimination between WT and mutant alleles, targeting the mutant allele exclusively.

source: The 17-Sg2 had higher cutting efficiency than 17-Sg1 and was chosen for further in vitro and in vivo experiments.

claim: Patient-derived iPSCs manifested a typical cobblestone-like morphology.
source: Patient-derived iPSCs manifested a typical cobblestone-like morphology (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Patient P1 carried the heterozygous variant c.50C>T (p.T17M) in RHO.
source: Sanger sequencing confirmed that patient P1 carried the heterozygous variant c.50C>T (p.T17M) in RHO (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Patient-derived iPSCs expressed human embryonic stem cell-specific surface antigens including NANOG, OCT4, TRA-1–60, and SSEA-4 proteins.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) staining showed that their iPSCs expressed human embryonic stem cell-specific surface antigens (International Stem Cell Initiative et al., 2007) including NANOG, OCT4, TRA-1–60, and SSEA-4 proteins (Figure 3E–H).

claim: The cutting efficiency of 17-Sg2 in patient-derived iPSCs was 3.94% as determined by Hi-Tom sequencing.

claim: 17-Sg2 did not facilitate SaCas9-mediated cleavage of the WT allele in normal donor iPSCs.

evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A 3bp-deletion (c.44_46del3bp) in the RHO-T17M allele was found in P1 iPSC colonies, whereas no indels were found in the RHO-WT allele.
source: To further confirm this allele-specific cutting, colonies from P1 iPS were picked and transfected with the 17-Sg2-Puro plasmid. Similarly, a cutting efficiency of 2.47% was detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), a 3bp-deletion (c.44_46del3bp) in the RHO-T17M allele was found, whereas no indels were found in the RHO-WT allele.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The allele-specific 17-Sg2 targeted the mutant allele specifically in patient-derived iPSCs.
source: These results firmly indicated that the allele-specific 17-Sg2 targeted the mutant allele specifically in patient-derived iPSCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results from iPSC experiments.

claim: GFP was expressed in the outer and inner segment (OS/IS) and outer nuclear layer (ONL) of photoreceptor cells at 1 mpi and 11 mpi.
source: IF analysis indicated that GFP was expressed in the outer and inner segment (OS/IS) and outer nuclear layer (ONL) of photoreceptor cells at 1 mpi and 11 mpi (Figure 4D).

claim: SaCas9 was present in injected retinas at 3 mpi at doses of 1×109 and 3×109.
source: WB analysis indicated that SaCas9 was present in injected retinas at 3 mpi (Figure 4G) at doses of 1×109 and 3×109.

source: T7E1 assay showed that SaCas9/17-Sg2 was able to cut the mutant sequence specifically (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).

evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Frameshift indels were expected to create a premature termination codon (PTC) and thereby resulted in the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of the edited RHO-5m mRNA.
source: We observed that 89.53% (77/86, TA and Sanger sequencing) of the indels were frameshift (Supplementary file 1c), which were expected to create a premature termination codon (PTC) and thereby resulted in the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of the edited RHO-5m mRNA (https://www.genecascade.org/MutationTaster2021).

claim: c.46_46delG (p. A16Rfs*32), the most common deletion, accounted for 20.93% (18/86) of all indels.

evidence: This is supported by T7E1 assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.
